alt: A quick guide for people who use drugs, detailing information about Tianeptine, its effects, risks, withdrawal, and overdose prevention.
summary:
This document, titled "Tianeptine: Quick Guide for People Who Use Drugs" by NEXT Distro, provides comprehensive harm reduction information regarding Tianeptine. It defines Tianeptine as an antidepressant with opioid effects, sold in various forms, and notes its historical uses for conditions like depression, anxiety, and ADHD, though it is now rarely prescribed due to side effects. The guide details the drug's effects, including light antidepressant effects at prescribed doses and sedation, muscle relaxation, euphoria, and rapid tolerance build-up at higher doses. It also outlines common and uncommon side effects, emphasizing the rapid increase in tolerance to opioid-like effects and potential allergic reactions.

The document highlights the legal status of Tianeptine, stating it is not a prescription drug in the United States, and contrasts typical prescribed doses in other countries with recreational doses which can be significantly higher. A critical section addresses routes of administration, strongly recommending oral use due to 99% absorption and warning against injecting or snorting, which can cause severe harm like vein collapse, necrosis, limb damage, and extreme pain. It also covers withdrawal symptoms, noting their similarity to opioid withdrawal but often being harsher, and provides guidance on withdrawal management through slow tapering.

Legally and medically, the document serves as a harm reduction tool, acknowledging the illicit use of Tianeptine and providing crucial safety information. It warns about overdose risks, particularly when mixed with antidepressants, MAOIs, or other depressants like alcohol, opioids, and benzodiazepines, due to the risk of cardiovascular problems and respiratory depression. The guide advises treating Tianeptine like an opioid, starting with low doses, and having naloxone available. It also provides contact information for NEXT Distro for further resources, underscoring its role in public health and drug safety education.

Tianeptine
Quick Guide for People Who Use Drugs

What is Tianeptine?
Tianeptine is an antidepressant with
opioid effects. Tianeptine is sold
in pills (ZaZa, Tianaa) and powder
(Tianeptine sulfate, Tianeptine sodium,
or Tianeptine Ethyl Ester).
Tianeptine has been used to treat depression, anxiety,
PTSD, IBS, asthma, fibromyalgia, and ADHD but it is rarely
prescribed nowadays due to side effects.
Effects
When used at the prescribed dose, it has light
antidepressant effects. In bigger doses, effects can
include sedation, muscle relaxation, short-lived euphoria,
stimulation, and rapid tolerance build-up. To many, the
euphoric effects are felt for about a minute if injecting it.
Side Effects
Most common: headache, dry mouth, dizziness,
constipation, insomnia, nightmares, and stomach pain/
aches. Uncommon: muscle aches, hot flashes, tremors,
palpitations, difficult or painful urination, and blurred
version. Continued use of tianeptine rapidly increases
tolerance to opioids like heroin, fentanyl, and morphine.
Rash, itching, swelling of the face or tongue, or difficulty
breathing can mean that you are allergic to Tianeptine.
Dose
Tianeptine is not a prescription drug in the United
States. The prescribed dose in other countries is usually
12.5mg three times a day for anxiety and depression.
Recreational or higher doses vary anywhere from 100mg
to multiple grams a day with tolerance. Tolerance to
tianeptine increases very rapidly with continued use.
Routes of Administration
Tianeptine is a hydrophobic (water insoluble/water
hating) drug, meaning it won't easily dissolve in water.
It is HIGHLY recommended that this drug only be
used orally. Tianeptine is 99% absorbed by the
body when eating it. Unlike other drugs, injecting or
snorting tianeptine will not get you higher than eating
it. When dissolved in water it turns glue-like and

injecting it may cause vein collapses, vein hiding, vein
swelling, and vein hardening much more frequently
compared with injecting traditional opioids. Injecting
Tianeptine pills can cause more harm than injecting
tianeptine powder and can result in necrosis (skin
rotting) and limb damage (may require amputation)
after heavy use. Many stop using tianeptine because
after injecting it they can no longer find a vein.
Snorting tianeptine is known to be very painful.
Withdrawal
Withdrawal from using 50mg a day for a month can last
about a week. Higher doses can make withdrawal more
intense and last up to 2 weeks. The most commonly
reported adverse effects consist of restless leg syndrome,
agitation, nausea, vomiting, increased heart rate, diarrhea,
tremors, and excessive sweating. Suicidal thoughts,
depression, insomnia, and cold/flu-like symptoms have
also been reported with Tianeptine withdrawals.
Withdrawal Management
If tapering off of tianeptine, slowly reduce your dose to
avoid withdrawal symptoms. The tianeptine withdrawal
is similar to an opioid withdrawal but considered to be
harsher for some. The withdrawal symptoms can be
managed like opioid withdrawals. Refer to the NEXT
opioid detox/withdrawal guide for more information
about withdrawal management.
Overdose Prevention
Mixing tianeptine with antidepressants or MAOI drugs
can lead to serious cardiovascular (heart) problems. Treat
tianeptine like an opioid. Start low and go slow when mixing
tianeptine with other depressant drugs like alcohol, opioids,
benzos, and alcohol because of the risk of respiratory
depression. Try not to use tianeptine alone and have
naloxone in-hand in case an overdose occurs. Overdoses
have been reported with as little as 300mg of tianeptine.
